title: Holiday Travel With Kids: A Pediatrician's Guide to Flying, Driving & Sick-Day Backup Plans (2026-27)
summary: A pediatrician's 2026-27 guide to holiday travel with kids: safe flying and driving, winter car-seat safety, and a clear sick-day plan for when your child gets sick away from home.
body_markdown:
Holiday travel with kids goes best when you prepare their health early, pack a simple travel medical kit, and know your sick-day backup plan before you leave. Book any needed vaccines and check-ups several weeks ahead. Bring the medicines and papers you may need. And learn the few warning signs that mean "go get care now." The rest of this guide walks through flying, driving, and what to do if your child gets sick far from home.

## Key Takeaways


- Book vaccines and check-ups early. Some shots need two doses several weeks apart, so plan before you travel.
- Ideally, wait until your baby is 2 to 3 months old before flying, when it's easier to protect a newborn from germs. Flying is generally safe from 7 days old if the trip can't wait (AAP).
- In winter, take the puffy coat off before you buckle the car seat. Bulky coats leave the harness too loose in a crash (AAP).
- If your child gets sick, there are four choices, not two: care at home, telehealth or your pediatrician, urgent care, or the ER.
- A baby under 3 months old with a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs the emergency room right away. A telehealth visit is not a substitute.


## Before You Go: The Pre-Travel Health Checklist


The best trip starts weeks before you pack. Get your child's health squared away early, refill any medicines, and build a small travel kit. A little planning now prevents most holiday health scrambles later.


### Vaccines and check-ups to schedule early (flu, COVID, RSV)


Book early because timing matters. Some vaccines need two doses spaced apart, and protection takes about two weeks to build. Waiting until the week you leave is too late.


Here's the flu timing every traveling family should know. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends a yearly flu shot for all children 6 months and older. Get it as soon as it's available, ideally by the end of October (AAP, 2026-2027 flu policy). Children 6 months through 8 years who are getting their very first flu shot, or who have had only one dose ever, need two doses at least 4 weeks apart. So a family leaving on November 20 who books the first dose on November 10 is not protected in time. Book early.


Flu season backs this up: flu usually peaks between December and February (CDC, 2025). That puts the busy Thanksgiving-to-New-Year travel window right as flu is climbing.


For COVID-19 and other routine shots, the simplest advice is also the safest: ask your pediatrician which vaccines your child should have before you travel, and book that visit early. Guidance can vary by child, so let your own doctor tell you what fits your child's age and health.


For young babies, ask about[RSV protection](https://blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/rsv-guide-from-a-pediatrician) , too. RSV season in most of the U.S. runs from about October through March, and there are ways to protect infants before it starts (CDC, 2025). Your pediatrician can tell you what your baby needs.


Not sure which shots your child needs before the trip?

### Refill prescriptions and pack a travel medical kit


Pack a travel medical kit so a small problem doesn't derail the trip. Think in three groups: papers, medicines, and supplies (CDC, Pack Smart).


Papers: copies of prescriptions, a copy of your child's immunization records, your insurance card, and a contact card that lists your child's conditions, medicines and doses, allergies, and your pediatrician's number. Also jot down the nearest urgent care and ER at your destination.


Medicines: children's pain and fever medicine (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), an antihistamine (for ages 6 months and up), motion-sickness medicine, and any prescriptions in their original labeled bottles. Pack enough for the whole trip plus extra in case of delays.


Supplies: a small first-aid kit, a thermometer, hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol or antibacterial wipes, and any rapid tests you use at home.


> "Always pack your at-home medical kit and strep tests. You won't regret it."
>
>
> Dr. Rachel Téllez, Blueberry Pediatrician


## Flying With Kids


Flying with kids is easier when you protect their ears, plan feedings, and know the right age for a newborn to fly. A few small steps prevent most in-flight tears.


### Ear pressure, feeding on takeoff/landing, and infant timing (AAP)


When can a newborn fly? The AAP suggests waiting until your baby is 2 to 3 months old before flying, though flying is generally safe once a baby is at least 7 days old (AAP, 2026). Airports and planes are crowded, and newborns catch things easily, so if the trip can wait a few weeks, let it.


Ease ear pain with sucking. Have your child nurse, take a bottle, or use a pacifier during takeoff and landing. Swallowing balances the pressure that makes ears hurt. Older kids can sip water or chew a snack.


A few more tips from the AAP:


- If your child had ear surgery or an ear infection in the 2 weeks before the trip, ask their doctor whether it's okay to fly.
- If your child has a cold or ear infection, a children's pain reliever may help. Follow the dosing directions carefully.
- Plane cabins are loudest at takeoff. Soft earplugs or noise-canceling headphones can protect a baby's hearing.


Don't use Benadryl to make a child sleep on a flight


Never give diphenhydramine (Benadryl) to sedate a child for travel without asking your pediatrician. It can cause serious side effects, and some children become more wound up, not sleepy.


Use a certified car seat on the plane when you can. For children, an FAA-approved car seat is the safest way to fly. Look for the label that says the restraint is certified for use in cars and aircraft. Turbulence is the leading cause of children's injuries on planes, and a harnessed seat protects your child. Booster seats can't be used on planes. Save those for the rental car.


Getting through security with a baby is easier than parents expect. Formula, breast milk, and the ice packs that cool them are allowed through the checkpoint in reasonable quantities. That is more than the usual limit on carry-on liquids. Pack them separately and tell the TSA officer at screening (TSA).


## Road Trips and Driving Safety


On the road, buckle car seats correctly, skip bulky coats in winter, and take regular breaks.


### Car seats, winter-coat safety, and break timing


The puffy-coat rule is the one many parents miss. In winter, take your child's thick coat off before buckling them into the car seat. Here's why it matters, in the AAP's own words:


Take the winter coat off before buckling


In a crash, fluffy padding in a coat flattens right away. That leaves extra space under the harness, and a child can slip through the straps and be thrown from the seat.


How to keep kids both warm and safe:


- Dress in thin layers: a close-fitting base layer, then pants and a warm top, then a thin fleece.
- Do the pinch test. If you can pinch the harness strap at the shoulder, it's too loose. Tighten it snug against the chest.
- Put the coat, or a blanket, over the buckled harness instead of under it. You can also put the coat on backwards over the straps.
- For babies, use the "plus-one" rule: one more layer than an adult would wear, but remove the coat and blanket before buckling.
- Keep an emergency bag in the car with extra blankets, dry clothes, hats, and snacks.


Take breaks and keep babies positioned safely. On a day drive, stop every 2 to 3 hours to feed and change your baby; overnight, every 4 to 6 hours (AAP). Keep the car seat[rear-facing](https://blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/rear-facing-car-seat-a-pediatricians-guide-for-parents) and installed at the angle the maker specifies. That angle keeps a baby's head from slumping chin-to-chest, which can block the airway. Babies can safely sleep in a correctly installed car seat while you drive, but a car seat is not a safe sleep space once you stop.


Never leave a child alone in a car


A car heats up fast, and heat stroke can happen quickly, even on a mild day and even for "just a minute." Take every child with you, every time.


## What to Do If Your Child Gets Sick While Traveling


If your child gets sick away from home, you have four choices, not two: care at home, telehealth or your pediatrician, urgent care, or the ER. Matching the sickness to the right level of care keeps your child safe without an unnecessary trip.


In our holiday-season telehealth visits, one of the most common calls comes from a worried parent. Their child spiked a fever far from home, and they aren't sure whether to rush to an ER. Most of the time, the honest answer is "not yet, but here's what to watch." That's the decision this section helps you make.


### When telehealth is enough vs. when to seek in-person/ER care


The AAP splits sick-day care into four settings. Here's how they map to travel:


If your child... Where to go


Is 3 months or older, has a fever with mild cold symptoms and good energy, and perks up with fluids and rest Care at home


Is drinking, breathing comfortably, and still interacting, but you want guidance Telehealth or call your pediatrician


Needs hands, eyes, or a swab: ear pain, a cut, a possible broken bone, flu symptoms while still drinking and breathing well. Have a Blueberry Medical Kit? For ear pain, record a short video of your child's ear drums with the kit's wireless ear scope (an at-home otoscope) and send it in the Blueberry app. A Blueberry pediatrician can review it by phone or chat, treat if needed, and tell you if your child still needs to be seen in person. Urgent care


Has trouble breathing, a seizure, a serious injury, is too weak to drink, or is under 3 months old with a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher Emergency room: go now


Start with a telehealth visit when your child is drinking, breathing comfortably, and still interacting with you. By phone or chat (with a quick photo or video upload if it helps), your pediatrician can check your child's energy, breathing, and overall state, and tell you whether you need to go somewhere in person. Telehealth is a good first call for mild illness, a flare-free chronic condition, follow-ups, and medicine questions.


Telehealth has limits, and it's important to know them. It's not enough when illness is moderate to severe, or when imaging or lab work is needed. It also falls short when the diagnosis needs a test or a close look. The AAP names urinary tract infections, strep throat, and ear infections as examples. This is where home tools help: a home strep test or a home otoscope (an ear-looking tool) lets your pediatrician see what they'd otherwise have to check in person. Blueberry's medical kit includes both, so a sore throat or an ear complaint can often be sorted out from your hotel room rather than in a waiting room. Some things still need a lab. A suspected urinary tract infection is one, and your pediatrician will tell you when that's the case.


> "If your child's at-home strep test results are positive, our pediatric team can immediately send an antibiotic prescription to a local pharmacy."
>
>
> Dr. Rachel Téllez, Blueberry Pediatrician


One travel rule surprises families: telehealth rules follow the patient, not the doctor. A clinician generally needs a license in the state where your child is at the time of the visit (HHS). So a pediatrician licensed only in your home state may not be able to see your child by video from Grandma's house two states away. Before you leave, check that your telehealth service covers the state you're visiting. (Blueberry families: Blueberry is available in all 50 states and Washington, DC, so you can be seen wherever you're traveling in the country.)


Watch for dehydration. It's the most likely reason a holiday trip ends at a clinic. Call your pediatrician if your child plays less than usual, has a dry mouth, makes fewer tears, or wets fewer diapers (for babies, fewer than six a day). In a baby, a sunken soft spot on top of the head is another sign to call about. Some signs mean your child needs to be seen right away rather than called about: sunken eyes; cool or blotchy hands and feet; wrinkled skin; unusual sleepiness; or urinating only once or twice all day. A road trip makes this easy to miss, because rest stops scramble your usual diaper count. On travel days, count wet diapers on purpose rather than going by feel.


Go to the ER if your child can't keep fluids down


If vomiting or diarrhea leaves your child too weak or too sleepy to drink, that's an emergency. Go to the emergency room.


## Managing Sleep, Routines, and Time Zones on the Road


Most U.S. holiday trips cross only one to three time zones, so the real challenge is a bumped routine, not true jet lag. Keep bedtimes and meals close to normal, and give kids time outside during the day.


True jet lag usually only kicks in when you cross more than three time zones (CDC). Think coast-to-coast or international trips. If your trip is that long, a few steps help:


- A few days before you go, shift bedtime an hour or two toward the new time zone.
- Once you arrive, switch to the local sleep and wake times right away.
- Get daylight during the day to help everyone's body clock catch up.
- Keep naps short, about 15 to 20 minutes, and offer plenty of water.


> "White noise machines are critical. They help block out the noise of hotels, so your kid (or you!) isn't woken up by people in the hallway."
>
>
> Dr. Kristen Borchetta, Blueberry Senior Physician Lead


If you're not sure the place you're staying has a safe crib for a baby, bring a portable play yard. A car seat, couch, or adult bed is not a safe sleep space for an infant.


## Preventing Illness While Traveling (Handwashing, Crowds, Germs)


The best way to keep kids healthy on a trip is the simple stuff: up-to-date shots, frequent handwashing, and cleaning surfaces you touch a lot. These habits lower your family's risk during the busy, germy holiday season (CDC, 2025).


- Wash hands often, especially before eating and after crowds, restrooms, or airport surfaces.
- Wipe down tray tables, armrests, and hotel remotes.
- If someone is sick, keep them away from others when you can, and get care early if your child is at higher risk for serious illness.
- In crowded places like airports, some families add masks or extra distance when a lot of illness is going around.


> "The only thing that changes when traveling by plane is the amount of disinfectant we carry. We bring a lot of hand sanitizer and disinfectant wipes for the airplane seat and trays."
>
>
> Dr. Melissa Tribuzio, MD, Board-Certified Pediatrician


## When to Call Your Pediatrician


Call your pediatrician right away if your child has a fever plus any warning sign, and go straight to the ER for the emergencies below. When in doubt, it's always okay to call.


The single most important line for parents of babies:


Fever in a baby under 3 months is an emergency


A baby under 3 months old with a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs in-person care right away. Go to the emergency room. This is true even if the baby looks fine, and it's true on vacation. A telehealth visit is not a substitute for the testing these babies need.


Call your pediatrician right away if your child has a fever along with any of these:


- Looks very ill, is unusually sleepy, or is very fussy
- A stiff neck, bad headache, severe sore throat or ear pain, trouble breathing, an unexplained rash, or repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- A weak immune system, or a heart condition
- A seizure, or a temperature above 104°F (40°C) that keeps coming back
- Still "acts sick" after the fever comes down, or seems to be getting worse


Also call if a[fever lasts more than 24 hours](https://blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/newborn-fever-when-to-worry-pediatricians-guide) in a child under 2, or more than 3 days in a child 2 or older.


Go to the ER (or call 911) right away for any of these:


- Trouble breathing: fast breathing, or the chest "pulling in" between the ribs (called retractions)
- Blue or gray lips, tongue, or face
- Very hard to wake, even with gentle shaking
- Vomiting so constant that no fluids stay down
- A stiff neck with sensitivity to light, or a sudden purple, bruise-like rash


Per the AAP, never 'wait and see' if your child's breathing suddenly worsens. Breathing changes can get worse within minutes, so seek care right away.


Remember: the exact temperature number matters less than how your child looks and acts. A calm, playful child with a fever is usually less worrying than a sluggish, floppy child with a lower fever.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How do I prepare my child's health before holiday travel?


Book any needed vaccines and a check-up several weeks early, refill prescriptions, and pack a travel medical kit. Ask your pediatrician which shots your child needs before you go. Some need two doses spaced weeks apart.


### What should be in a travel medical kit for kids?


Papers (prescriptions, immunization records, insurance card, a contact card), medicines (children's fever/pain medicine, antihistamine, motion-sickness medicine, prescriptions in original bottles), and supplies (first-aid kit, thermometer, hand sanitizer, rapid tests).


### Is it safe to fly with a newborn, and when?


The AAP suggests waiting until your baby is 2 to 3 months old, though flying is generally safe once a baby is at least 7 days old. Because airports and planes are crowded, delay a few weeks when you can to protect your newborn from illness.


### How do I keep my child's ears from hurting on a flight?


Have your child nurse, take a bottle, or use a pacifier during takeoff and landing. Older kids can sip water or chew a snack. Swallowing balances the pressure that causes ear pain.


### Why should I remove my child's winter coat before buckling the car seat?


In a crash, a puffy coat flattens instantly and leaves the harness too loose, so a child can slip out. Dress kids in thin layers and put the coat over the buckled harness instead.


### How often should we stop on a road trip with kids?


For babies, stop every 2 to 3 hours during the day and every 4 to 6 hours overnight to feed and change them. Everyone benefits from regular breaks to stretch and rest.


### What do I do if my child gets sick away from home?


Match the illness to one of four levels: care at home, telehealth or your pediatrician, urgent care, or the ER. Start with telehealth if your child is drinking, breathing comfortably, and still interacting. Go straight to the ER for trouble breathing, a seizure, or a baby under 3 months with a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher.


### How do I keep kids from getting sick while traveling?


Keep vaccines up to date, wash hands often, and wipe down high-touch surfaces like tray tables and hotel remotes. Keep sick family members apart when possible, and get care early for higher-risk children.


Medical disclaimer: This guide is general information, not medical advice for your specific child. For concerns about your child's health, contact your pediatrician, and seek emergency care for any warning sign above.
